short: An 80-mile stone wall marked Rome's most heavily fortified land frontier for nearly three centuries.
full:
Hadrian ordered the wall built from 122 CE, running roughly 73 miles (80 Roman miles) coast to coast across northern Britain from the Solway Firth to the Tyne. Three legions took about six years to raise a stone and turf barrier studded with milecastles, turrets and sixteen major forts, formalising a frontier Hadrian preferred to fixed, defensible limits rather than further costly conquest.

The wall was briefly superseded by the more northerly Antonine Wall from the 140s but was reoccupied as the effective frontier once that line was abandoned around 162. Garrisoned continuously, it regulated trade and movement as much as it repelled attack, and it remained in use into the early fifth century as Roman authority in Britain collapsed. It survives as the best-preserved Roman frontier monument in the empire and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
